The numerical preponderance, therefore, as the reader will see, is on the side of the Scandinavians or Danes. The Scandinavian King, who thus promulgated a constitution for his subjects, is Duke of Holstein, of Laueuburg, and of Schleswig, but King of Denmark. Among the majority of his Scandinavian subjects the sway ol Fueiuorik \ II., was loyally acknowledged and his constitution gratefully received. o iso plan times. Liverpool, April 17, 1850. The West India Association Memorial to Government. The following documents, the first addressed to Parliament, the second to the colonial minister, Lord Grey, emanate from the West India Association, and are pregnant with great facts. The humble Petition of the West India Merchants, Planters, and others at the Port of Liverpool, Showeth, þÿ That the West India colonies, while protected by the laws of the mother country, possessed a high value; and, until their power of production was impaired by legislative acts of the Imperial Parliament, furnished a superabundant supply of sugar for the use of this country. That, when the people of this country determined to abolish slavery, which they had themselves instituted, the most earnest representations were made on behalf of those colonies, urging their just claims to full compensation, and the great hazard to which plantation property would he exposed, unless sullicient arrangements were made for maintaining its regular cultivation. That, when Parliament, disregarding the colonists' fears, thought lit to pass the abolition act, it admitted their claim to compensation þÿ tirst, in a limited grant of money ; second, in a modified service of the emancipated slaves for six years ; and, in the expression of the nation's abhorrence of slavery, gave the strongest assurance that they would be protected from unequal competition, and more especially with countries which are cultivated by slaves and carry on the slave trade.

That, the slaves of our West India colonics were valued by commissioners appointed by the crown at £43,104,889 8s. 1 Id., from which amount, however, the commissioners of compensation, without hearing any argument in behalf of the colonists, deducted £5,430,558 16s 3d., and ultimately allotted to the West India proprietors only £16,639,937 8s. 4Jd. That this valuation did not apply to more than one-third of the property affected by the abolition act, the land, with the buildings and machinery, which became unavailable without continuous labour at a reasonable rate, having been left entirely out of consideration.

That, notwithstanding the solemn declaration of an act of Parliament, the apprenticeship was so interfered with in 1838, by resolutions of t he House of Commons, as to force that probationary term to an end two years before the allotted period. That, while the colonies were labouring in the great experiment, under such inconsiderate changes, they were exposed in quick succession þÿ first, to the full competition of the produce of British India, next to that of every country possessing the semblance of freedom : and, finally, in 1846, though the most positive assurances had been given by Parliament in 1844, that the produce of all slave countries would continue to be excluded, was passed the act 9 and 10 Victoria, Chap. 63, for the admission of sugar, tiie produce, not only of countries maintaining the most rigorous slavery, but likewise of countries carrying on the slave trade in defiance of treaties which bound them to suppress it. That, the landed property of the West India colonics lias been thus rendered by the legislative acts generally valueless, for, hirge as is their declared production, it is very considerably less than in 1834, the last year of slavery ; and it appears by a return ordered by the House of Commons that, comparing the imports from British Guiana, Jamaica, and Trinidad, during 1 n the vears 1834 to 1838, (the year when apprenticeship was abruptly terminated,) with those of the years 1844 to 1848, the production of sugar lias fallen off 3,130,000 cwts.

Molasses 506,433 cwts. Runt 3,324,627 galls. Coffee 52,661,350 lbs. and the production of cotton lias entirely ceased, neither can it he allowed that quantity presents any criterion of cost, which your petitioners are prepared to prove before a committee of your honourable House, exceeds 1 lie value of the production in the great majority of these colonies. Your petitioners do not presume to question the right of Parliament to alter the public policy of this country affecting them in common with other British subjects, but they respectfully assert that it is inconsistent with justice, as w ell as with the practice of the constitution, first to invade property on the plea of a national aversion from slavery, and then to consummate its destruction by supporting slavery and the slave trade in other countries, unless the contradictory policy be accompanied by adequate compensation not only for the value of the slaves, but also for the deterioration of the freeholds to which they were attached. Without such compensation, proprietors in the West India colonies will have been as completely despoiled of their property as though it had been directly confiscated, thus establishing a precedent hitherto unknown to British legislation, and dangerous to the stability of all property. Your petitioners, therefore, earnest'v pray your honourable House to adopt

those measures which justice requires to restore to the British West India colonists the value of their property, sacrificed to a great national undertaking, either by such arrangements as will secure them an ample supply of free labourers at a moderate rate, or by awarding them a full measure of pecuniary compensation ; and your petitioners are urged the more at this moment to implore your honourable House, in consistent unison with its recent decision, not to relax the measures requisite to put an end to the slave trade, at once to relieve them from ruinous competition with the slave dealer, by prohibiting the consumption in Great Britain of sugar and coffee produced by countries where the slave trade is still carried on, it being universally believed that Cuba and the Itrazils would long ago have abandoned slavery and the slave trade, had not Great Britain decidedly encouraged and stimulated their continuance by opening her market to their cheap sugar. And your petitioners will ever pray &c. On behalf of the petitioners, F. SHAN!), Chairman of the West India Association of Liverpool.

To the Right Honourable Earl Grey, Secretary of State for the Cabinet. The Memorial of the West India Association of Liverpool, on behalf of the Merchants, Planters, and others interested in the Colony of British Guiana, Jlumhlv showcth, þÿ That the colony of British Guiana, from being the most prosperous, is become the most distressed of any of her Majesty's possessions. That, after the emancipation of the slaves, the planters were prevented importing free labourers in sufficient numbers to supply the colony with continuous labour, and the consequence is that the production of sugar lias largely lallcn off; cotton and coffee (originally forming the principal export of the colony) have been almost abandoned ; and land sufficient to supply England with cotton, of a superior quality to American, allowed to run waste. That the British Guiana planters arc in a state of the greatest distress. In 1838 there were '258 estates in Demcrara and Essequibo in profitable cultivation ; of these, 71 have been abandoned, 111 sold under execution sale, þÿ all occasioned, as now clearly appears, by the emancipation of the negroes without allowing the planters to supply themselves with labourers from other sources. The inhabitants of British Guiana arc obliged to receive the produce of countries where the slave trade is carried on, whilst they see their own fertile soil rendered of no value for want of a sufficient number of labourers to cultivate it. That the colonists of British Guiana
arc thus absolutely prevented trying the rrcat experiment of free labour against slave labour; and tliey ask but to be allowed that to which they conceive they have a right, and which is granted

to 0 JR 0 2 ATI 3. to British subjects elsewhere þÿ the free importation of labourers willing to emigrate from all parts of the world. Your memorialists cannot more strongly express their opinion of what Demerara is capable of becoming, than by quoting the words of Sir J. C. Smith, the late Governor of Demerara. " If (said he) I live to get regular a stream of emigration from India into this magnificent province, with a moderate sujiply from Africa and elsewhere, I will make it the first colony under the British crown I will make it a second India." : That your memorialists would refer your lordship to the period (not very long since) when only (id, 000 bales of cotton were annually imported into England, of which two-thirds tame from Guiana and the West Indies þÿ not one bale from the United States ; whereas now the cotton manufacturers in Lancashire are reducing their mills to short time, not because there is want of a demand for tw ist, but because a doubt exists whether America, into whose hands the cotton cultivation is thrown, can spare sufficient for England from her own increasing consumption, the juice of cotton has advanced 40 per cent, in contemplation of short supply. Such could not have happened had the cultivation of cotton in Demerara been encouraged. Your memorialists feel that they have n just and undeniable claim for a snjqily of labourers ; and they submit that the most natural source is Africa þÿ a country filled with an unemployed population within twenty days' sail of British Guia-

na, the climate the same temperature, but more healthy. Gentlemen acquainted with the African coast, and in no way connected with the West Indies, state that by encouraging free interchange of the negroes between Africa and t lie West Indies, a stoji would he jmt to the slave trade, and the jieojile of Atricu would he civilised. þÿ Stramlgaden Fifty large vessels trade between Liverpool and Africa ; they enter into contracts for five years with labourers on the Kroo roast to go to the British factories on the Bonny River, from which place tlicy return at the end of the time greatly improved by their Lssociation with British subjects. Black seamen are emjiloyed to assist to navigate our ships from Africa to England. A small vessel, 102 tons, arrived in Liverpool lately, which had carried (53 black jieojile from Bonny River to the Kroo coast þÿ a longer voyage than to Demerara. This vessel would not have been permitted to convey these people to Demerara! It is fifteen years since a slaver entered the Bonny River, and yet, at this time, the inhabitants of that river arc prevented going to Demerara. LETTER FROM PROFESSOR WEBþÿSTER S DAUGHTER. From the Manchester. (Mass.) Messenger. The following communication from a daughter of Professor Webster, in reply to a letter addressed her, has been handed us by the gentlemen to whom it was directed : þÿ Cambridge, April 8, 1850. Dam el M \rsh, Esq. þÿ Sir: þÿ I, this morning, received the very kind letter vou addressed tome, and which I hasten to answer, to thank you in the name of my mother, my sisters and myself, fur 1he true sentiments you entertain respecting my beloved father. You believe him innocent, and you believe what is true : he is the victim of circumstances ; a deeply injured man þÿ that he is innocent, we his family know, and nothing on earth will ever take from ns this conviction. YVe have never, from the moment he was snatched from his home, had a shadow of a doubt on our minds, and whatever the world may say or do, we shall ever have that feeling to support us. The knowledge of his innocence supported my father during the hours of suffering in the Court room; that it is that gives him and us calmness now, amidst the many sources of sorrow that have overwhelmed us. Far different from what we anticipated, was the result of the trial, for we had been assured throughout ihc winter that our father could riot but be restored to us. and, that at the trial he must receive justice for the many wrongs that had been heaped upon him. But justice tied from the court room, and prejudice took her place. Yet hope still lingers with us, for we

trust that the public voice rvill be raised against the gross injustice that has been committed, and w ill not allow our country to bear such a stigma on her name, such an everlasting stain, as will be that of the sacrifice of one so truly innocent as my father. And if one w ord from us, sir, can add a þÿfeather weight s to the efforts that are being made þÿ Oh, may We give you the deep assurance of our hearts, that we feel grateful for the interest that you express and feel, and for what you are doing in our behalf. þÿ May God, in his infinite mercy, look down upon you and bless the efforts that are being made, and if it is not his will to bring the truth to light, and to allow

sf, a via this awful mystery to be explained, may ( he enlighten the minds of those into 1 whose hands the case will pass. 1 must again thank you, sir, for the kind feeling you express towards my dear father. Nothing that the world ; respectfully begs h ave to communicate, can do now, gives us greater consolation than the knowledge that others i believe him innocent. Sympathy has llowed abundantly from many hearts towards us, his iamiiy, but how much more prized by us is that sympathy, i when expressed for him. That our ! beloved father may be restored to us, j is the fervent prayer of our hearts and we wait trembling in tire hope, that j those who are now to decide in this i case may see the terrible injustice that has been committed, and has inflicted no much suffering on so many. SWITZERLAND. After a discussion, which has occupied three sittings, the National Council of Berne has just decreed, by a majority of 64 to 36, that the French monetary system shall be carried out in Switzerland. Various reports are afloat respecting a friendly writing from the Emperor of Russia to onr King. We of course J know nothing of the contents of this letter, but we believe that we can say with certainty that such regulations have been made on the part of our Government as shall provide for every eventuality. The Danish Schleswig deputation left Copenhagen on the 23rd nil. for Fredericksborg, where they were received very (graciously) by his Majesty. After the audience they accompanied his Majesty to view the principal parts of his palace, and afterwards had the honour of dining with him. The Laudsthing decided, by 81) votes against 2, that the interpellation of Dr. Paulsen, respecting the llolstein deputation, should take place on the 24th. þÿ The substance of the interpellation was whether the llolstein deputies were commissioned by the member of the Stadthalterschafi, whether they came or in a private capacity ; and, secondly, whether the Danish Government intended to enter into any negotiation with them. The Ministerial President replied that the gentlemen who had arrived from Ilolstein had declared in writing that they were not delegates of the Sladtlialterschaft ; and further, that

they did not come with the mandate of any authority corporation in Holstcin. or It was of course impossible for the Government to enter into official negotiations with private persons. Rut as the Government felt justified in regarding the presence of these men as a proof that not an inconsiderable number of his Majesty's subjects, who were placed in so unhappy a position to him, cherished the sincere desire to seek peace and reconciliation, the Government could not take on itself the responsibility of refusing to listen to the attempt made towards a reconciliation. The Ministerial President added that the Government, as a matter of course, could negotiate only on the basis of the convention of the 10th of July, 184!).

DARMSTADT. The Muriier of the Countess Goritz. þÿ This deeply interesting trial, which occupied the unusual term of 34 days, is concluded. The foreman of the jury, in answer to the several indictments, declared that the footman of the count, Johannes Staulf, was guilty of the murder. The President sentenced Johannes Stanff to imprisonment for life, with payment of five-sixths of the costs. His father, llenry StaulF, was sentenced to six months, and his brother, Jacob Staulf, to three months' imprisonment, for being abettors, and concealing the stolen property.

POLAND. The administrative Council for the kingdom of Poland has issued an edict to all the authorities in regard to the Polish Jews, desiring that those Jews who have not yet adopted the national costume, but have retained their peculiar dress, shall not be compelled to do so, but shall pay the tax upon dress. The Rerlin news-letters state that 80, (KK) percussion muskets have been distributed among the Russian regiments 111 Poland.

RUSSIA. The late martial news from Russia is Still confirmed by all the German and Austrian papers. The Russian troops on the frontiers of Prussia are quoted at 160,000 men, and strong reinforcements are said to he marching up. 50, (KM) among them are Rashkir and Circassian horsemen.

The Widow and her Son. þÿ Considerably more than half a century ago there dwelt in a small borough of Forfarshire 1 poor widow, who earned a humble but respectable livelihood for herself and her onlv son by keeping a stall, principally for the sale of crockeryware, in the market-place. It was a time when gentlemen lived harder than they do now ; and, although the word " Watert'ordising" had not been invented, the thing implied by it was greatly in vogue. The townspeople then were not unaccustomed to the occasional freaks and rough practical jokes of a neighbouring gentleman, who had lately succeeded to enormous property and a peerage, and there was no particular surprise manifested when, late one evening, the humble stall of the widow was overturned in an after-dinner frolic, and the brittle ware it contained smashed upon the street. The aggressor was Lord Panmure. Next morning the proprietress of the stall waited upon his lordship, and the claim for damages was soon settled to the satisfaction of all parties.

3 © 3a ® 1 AT !3» " And now, my good woman," said the overthrower of the crockeryware, " is there anything else I can do for you?" The widow replied that she had an only son, a sharp little fellow, whom she wished to see receiving a better education than her limited means enabled her to bestow 011 him. Lord Panmure at once promised the necessary aid. lie was as good as his word. Little Joey was sent for. The intelligence and sharpness of the boy were readily recognised and highly commended, and he was at once placed in an excellent school. Such was the curiously-caused commencement of a long career of industry and honour. The little boy, the poor widow's son, was Joseph Hume. þÿ

The A e n Steamship City of Glasgow. The City of Glasgow, commanded by

peller steamship. The Glasgow Count uk, of the Kith March gives the following description of her : This splendid steamship, (the City of Glasgow), which was launched so recently as the '28th l'ebruarv, sets out today, at one o'clock, as our readers are

tie þÿ being the first attempt to establish steam communication between this city and the commercial capital of the I nited States. Although the Citv of Glasgow only left the building yard at the period specified, she has, to a certain extent, earned the character of a tried ship, before being applied to the great work for which she is destined. Simultaneously with the construction of the iron hull, the machinery was being prepared in the engine foundry of Messrs. Tod A Macgregor, the builders: and, as a consequence, the steam was up within little more than a fortnight after the ship left the stocks. She was immediately sent to sea on a private but effectual trial trip, and for several days encountered, and well w ithstood, all the wild blasts of the equinox, which were felt so smartly along the west coast, during the middle and close of March. The propel-

ceeded expectation; but, as the sailing qualities of the ship are now lo be tested bv the sweep across the Atlantic, it will be well to wait for the result, as it will be narrated in the log of Captain Matthews. Since the return of the Citv, she has been berthed on the south side, completing her internal furnishings, engaging passengers, and taking in cargo. But during this time, and especially for the last few days, the ship has been visited by thousands on thousands of our population þÿ ladies and gentlemen, strangers as well as towns' folk þÿ and she lias been converted into the scene of a gay I promenade from morning to night. The ship is as strong as iron plates, bars, straps, and rivets can make her; and I she is divided into two water-tight com- | partments, which would secure her j against almost every contingency of accident, excepting that of being throw n bodily upon the rocks. But, to avert any risk of this kind, a gentleman lias been engaged as commander, who should know the course between Great Britain and America almost as well as if mile-

stones had been placed along the road þÿ viz., Captain Matthews þÿ w ho has crossed the Atlantic iff) times as an officer, and 20 of these as commander of the favorite Great Western þÿ a gentleman, who by the testimony of all who have sailed with him, is entitled to the character of " every inch a seaman." The hands to be directed by this able head appear plement to make up a very adequate com- þÿ there being in all devoted exclusively to the business of the ship, first, second, and third officers, 20 seamen, 4 engineers, !) firemen, and 5 appr entices; while to minister to the wants of the passengers there are 12 stewards, 2 stewardesses, I baker, 1 cook, 4 assistants, a band of musicians, with brass and stringed instruments: and lastly a doctor, with an ample medicine chest þÿ a functionary, however, who is in the meantime kept in the background, for it is not conceived that any one can be, or should be, ill, w hen so many appliances are at han'd to keep them well. The City of Glasgow has been laid out for 1 10 berths, viz. ,52 of the first class abaft the funnel, and 58 of the second class before the funnel. Every one of these lias been engaged from Mr. Langlands, the intelligent agent, by passengers of both sexes, from every part of the three aware, on her voyage across the Atlan- j kingdoms, but principally from Scotland. The passage money is 20 guineas for the first class, and 12 guineas for the second. After accommodating the passengers, the ship has room for lOt 0 tons of cargo,

which is already largely occupied by nuimtfucluivd goods, the produce of Glasgow. To make ail sale as precaution can make it, we may mention fla t the ' City" carries six bouts, viz., two life boats, two cutters, and two gigs, which in all arc commodious enough to carry 200 persons. The internal fittings are tasteful and genteel, and got up with a view to comfort and pleasantness, rather than to dazzle w ith unprofitable brilliancy. The grand saloon is upwards of 54 feet long, fitted up with rich wainscot panelling þÿ the ornamental part in the Rennnisance style, being richly carved. Along the sides are 12 large pictures, representing striking views in various countries. As the anticipated success and relative speed of the City of Glasgow will be watched with considerable interest, we may mention that, on Saturday next, the 20th iiist., the Canada leases Liverpool, and the W ashington from Southampton, both direct for New York.

To the Proprietor and Editor of the "St. Croix Avis." , Air EDITOR. At 110 inconsiderable expense, the community at large purchased of the deceased Mr. It. Beatt.y a on erected a Prison þÿ part of the Estate Richmond, say 80 Acres, and þÿ a kind of penetentiary under therethe consolatory assurance of its proving a terror to the culprit, the disorderly, and the disobedient, the means whereby this was bought to pass were strenuous coercive labor and isolation at night ; and during certain intervals at day. The last named measure is undoubtedly practised; but in regard to the first we cannot than think otherwise, for assuredly it is no punishment in employing an offender, or him who slii'ks bis work, in the cutting of grass; cultivating ground provision; in raising a few vegetables, and but occasionally mending the þÿstreets the latter cektfs the most suitable occupation þÿ for which l>e is rloathed and housed, and when ill, provided with medicine, nourishment and medical attendance at the public expense. I was therefore somewhat elated, deeming it an amended state of things, when on Wednesday 1 perceived a considerable body of offenders employed in mending one of the principal streets damaged by the flood of rain which fell oil the preceding þÿday for all appeared to have turned out. Well Sir! tins opinion was rather strengthened on Thursday when I heard of several Householders being called on, each for a quota, to Hire additional bands, for in tny ignorance I imagined the jail birds were deemed insufficient, and as the town bad suffered much

those were deemed essential to the energetic prosecution of the work. It bad the appearance of vitality in the body corporate, so I bailed it as a harbinger of better state of things þÿ first, that the prisoners were less than hitherto, and secondly, that one and all of them consequently, would be thus sedulously employed for so legitimate a purpose and that hereafter we might not be reproached for our filthy streets. Conceive my mortification, therefore on Friday, when I was told I was mistaken; that the prison contained its usual number of inmates ; that a number were taken off' and sent to cut grass and were to continue so occupied, that the repairs would jog on as Hitherto ; and that in all likelihood the assessment of 32 cents would be persisted in. This I consider a grievance that should be remedied, for is it not notorious that, as a body, no part of the community has suffered and still suffer like the major.ly of House-owners; in being taxed disproportionately high ; their rents low, and their chief means of subsistence taken from them by the " Act of Emancipation" so that not a few are straightened to meet the annual tux' and many from absolute p< verty are tlireathrn»'d to tie houseless. Let me therefore sol.cit inquiry whether it would not be more to the purpose to keep the prisoners repairing the streets, and when well finished hire them out to the respective estates even to inend the highways, than to employ them as heretofore and to (arm out the grass to the highest bidder, or sell the land.

DENMARK. The negotiations going on between Denmark and Prussia do not scent to us, as far as we can penetrate the intrigue, to be sincerely promoted by Prussia. þÿ At present it is difficult to judge; but there is a want of straightforward honesty in the proceedings which makes us fear, unless a Russian fleet appears in the sound, that Prussia will only amuse Denmark until she is sufficiently strong to defy her once more. Prussia pursues her own schemes of with inflexible ambition.
Tiif. Danes in Copenhagen. þÿ The Danes appear to strangers a lively, joyous, life-enjoying and in the highest

3 U' » Dis b !t Z. A T 1 3» degree excellent and amiable people, open hearted, sympathetic and ready to oblige. In many respects they remind one of the Athenians, lor Copenhagen with its stirring and vivacious popu lace, its museums, its gallerie ; and its artists, its learned men and their lectures, its theatre life, and the people's enjoyment of it, may well he styled the modern Athens. Copenhagen bears the same relation to Denmark that Paris does to France. It is the centre, the organic point of the nation, where the life and soul have their seat. A silent company in Stockholm would actually be confounded at the bustle and loud loquacity in the drawing-rooms of Copenhagen. This produces not a harmonious hut a lively effect, while the frank kindness which is shown to the stranger cannot hut present life to him in a pleasant aspect. If one wishes to become acquainted with the amiable disposition of the Danish people, one must go into the street, amongst the people, amongst those who are called the rabble, see them in their traffic and mutual intercourse, talk with them, ask one's way, and so on, and the stranger will be amazed at the good will, the politeness, and the readiness to oblige, which he will meet with, until he is compelled to say, " there is no rabble in Copenha-

The King of Denmark has presented Mr. J. R. Hind with a gold medal, for the discovery of the comet of February (5, 1847. Mr. Himl has also received from the Academy of Sciences, at Paris, a prize on the Lelande foundation, for 1 lie discovery of Iris and Flora in the year 1847. »«« WEST INDIES. The advices received by the Civile steamer from the West India Islands present very little news of interest. þÿ The principal subject referred to in Jamaica letters is the introduction of Dr. Scoflern's process for improving the manufacture of sugar by means of salts of lead. A sample of sugar by this process is represented to he of a fine, large, strong grain, and nearly as white as ordinary refined, sugar; it is said to he quite practicable to render it as white as the best double refined. Trade was still very dull in the island. Various abandoned estates have been sold for the non-payment of taxes, &.C., and many more are at the present period under sequestration. The committee appointed by the two houses of legislature of Montserrat to inquire into the state of the country had delivered their report, and state that, collected from the best information, it is reduced to the lowest ebb of misery and wretchedness. The colonists of Trinidad were desirous of having an elective legislative council in lieu of the present form of aggrandisement government, and w ere about to petition the home government on the subject. At Grenada an excessive drought from which the island had suffered so long
and so much had been partially relieved by a few showers of rain, which promis-

ed to continue. In some localities the canes had been completely scorched, and rendered almost useless lor the production of sugar, which caused fears that the cultivation of next year would he completely destroyed, hut which the rain alluded to was only in time to save. At Rorbice, during the month of March and the early part of April, a great quantity of rain had fallen, which had quite swamped some plantations þÿ Tlia crops had been entirely lost, and a scarcity of ground provisions was later in the month expected. þÿ Bell's Messenger

From this point of time, the French Minister at Athens, and the French Government at Paris, had a full right to conceive that the affair with Greece had become a joint negotiation. Whence, then, says the French minister, lias it happened that wc now see a separate signature and an exclusive agreement, þÿ one w hich entirely excludes the French mediation, and disclaims the authority and influence of France in a matter of her Own concern and common protectorship of Greece? Is not this an injurious contempt, not to say a positive insult to the dignity of France, in the eyes of Russia and Europe ! Is it not an unfair dealing, and an especial breach of the confidence which should exist between friends and mediators ? To this, as we understand, Lord Palmcrston's reply has been, that when the friendly offices of France were first accepted, it was under the express understanding that the whole affair should he considered as the concern of England only; and that the good offices of the French Minister should he confined singly to the functions of reciprocally abating the requisitions of the one party, and the pertinacious resistance of the other. It was thus understood, that the functions of a mediator should never pass into those of an arbitrator, and that

England should retain throughout, with out giving any offence to France, her own full right of admitting, qualifying, or rejecting any terms or offers proposed. Electric Telegraph across the Atlantic. The New York papers give full particulars of Mr. John Wilkes's plan for forming a line of electric telegraph between North America and Europe þÿ for carrying out w hich a company is stated to he forming iu that city. He proposes to lay down at the bottom of the sea a wire of solid iron, well insulated, from the eastern coast of Newfoundland to the western coast of Ireland. On the good anchoring ground which lies 590 miles distant from the first of these countries he will establish a repeating station, by which the length of wire will be reduced to 1G99 English miles. þÿ However deep may be the Atlantic, he proposes to conduct his wire along its bottom. According to all appearances, he says, the depth nowhere exceeds two miles, and he has reason to believe that it is little more than one. þÿ But even supposing there may be submarine valleys of 19 or 20 miles in depth and 50 or 00 in width, he is of opinion thai such hollows would present no

great obstacle, as the wire might he made to pass over them by rneas of supports fixed (we are not told how) at intervals of two miles or less, so that the wire should he kept always 200 fathoms below the surface of the sea. þÿ Every 100 miles he would anchor a small raft with mast and flag, communicating with the wire, that the latter may be taken up when requiring to be repaired or renewed ; but his opinion is, that there is no possibility of a wire laid at such a depth being injured. To lay down this telegraphic line, two ships working by a very simple process of machinery will, he says, suffice. The work will be done in two years, and will cost about 700,000 dols. þÿ Ibid. Callioan- The European Times of the 20th March, contains the following, relative to Mr. Calhoun's death: þÿ The news of Mr. Calhoun's death arrived this week, and, although the melancholy event was partially anticipated by the hopeless state in which the last accounts left him, yet such an exit is too important in itself and bears too closely upon the conflict still pending between the Northern and the Southern States, to pass away without attracting considerable attention. Mr. Calhoun has been a leading politician during the greater part of two generations. His public talents brought him prominently before his countrymen; and the distinguished part which he played in the great questions of the day, combined with the impetuosity of his temperament, rendered him, par excel-

lence, the embodiment of Southern character. It was always felt that during his lifetime, any compromise on the slave question was perfectly unattainable. What effect his disappearance may have on the state of parties, cannot of course, be immediately ascertained; but the tone of the papers in the great Northern cities induces us to believe that the slave party deprived of a leader in whose abilities they placed implicit confidence may desire, as far as possible, to narrow the breach with their northern fellow-citizens. We hope it may be so, albeit the authorities on which we base this opinion arc not the most reliable in a question so delicate and excitable as the question of slavery. Whatever differences of opinion may prevail respecting the views of the late American statesman, we happen to know, through a confidential channel, so many amiable traits in his private life, as to make us feel a deeply personal respect for the man. The union has produced some great men, and amongst them, certainly not the least able and respected was J. C. Calhoun.

The inhabitants of the AVest Indies will he agreeably astonished to learn that by very recent explorings, deposits of gold have been found in the rivers of the eastern vallies of Venezuela, which promise to lie as prolific in their yield as any which have been discovered in California. The extracts which we have made thereon, enter so fully upon tiie matter, that we find very little left for us to say on the subject, except that we may express a hope that these immense treasures which evidently yet lie hidden in the soil of South America, will not he permitted long to remain so. Already many of our young men are talking of an early rip t to the "diggings," and there is some probability of a company being organised here to carry on the washing for gold dust þÿ (which, it is stated, is likely to prove the most productive mode of amassing the precious metal) þÿ in a more systematic and expeditious manner than could be effected by individual enterprise. auriferous grounds already visited by other people last year. than 1 .70 ounces. They tire composed of gold dust and of grains of various sizes; of this last there may be twenty ounces, which may he truly compared to lentils and grains of coffee. There are also some of a larger size, and even of above half an ounce in weight. To Ibis may he added also some apprehension on the part ol Mr. Monasterio, who, with onlytwo companions could scarcely consider himself safe in those wilds in company

with peons. The bark Carlota, Captain Gerard, arrived on Sunday from Porto llico. She brings us further intelligence from Mayaguez. It is of considerable interest. W e learn from Captain G., that the schooner North Carolina, (.'apt. lleachcr, was a total wreck, and that Captain It. and crew, at the risk of their lives, saved chronometer, spy glass and charts, which were taken away from them by the Spanish authorities, besides their clothing. The latter, upon being exam- j ined had found to be of no value, was returned. The captain and crew were then forbidden to leave the island, at the risk of being imprisoned. What part the American Consul took at this affair, is unknown, but it is said he prefered furnishing the crew board and lodging; saying that the American government did not allow to American citizens in distress, in foreign ports, but forty cents a day, which, he said, would not support them in Mayagucz, and if he found them with board, he would have to pay for it out of his own pocket. The poor fellows were therefore obliged | to depend upon the charily of the Ante- j rican and English vessels in port, and, for upwards of a month, they would he from one vessel to another þÿ for as soon as an American vessel would he ready for sea, she would be strictly overhauled by the vigilant Captain of the Port, who, it he found cither the captain, mate, or any of the crew on hoard would order them, hag and baggage, on shore, like so many J dogs. o I On the 11th of April, the U. S. sloop-

of-war Albany, Commander Randolph, arrived. The next day Captain Bencher reported his barbarous treatment to Captain Randolph, who was at the time in the American þÿConsul office. s Captain Randolph said: þÿ Sir. þÿ I will not leave this island until i you get satisfaction, and I will send you j and your crew home soon. Some Spanish loafer who happened to be in the þÿConsul office s at the time, communicated what Captain Randolp had said to the Captain of the Port, who immediately had the Captain, mate, and two of his crew, arrested by soldiers, and dragged to prison like so many felons, lie, then made his boast if the Captain of the Yankee man-of-war wanted his countrymen, to come ashore and j get them. The next day, early in the j morning, Captain Randolp had his ship hauled in as close as possible, the þÿship s guns all loaded and ready for action, and then sent ashore, by his 1st Lieut., Mr. Ridgelv, a letter to the commander-inchief, stating if the men were not given up, he would fire upon the town. The town was immediately in commotion, and the men given up in somewhat of a hurry. It was the intention of Captain

Randolph to demand the captain's chronometer, spy-glass, and charts. It is highly important that American men-ol-war should frequent the island of Porto Rico, for the abuses and barbarities practised on American citizens are intolerable.
The Captain of the Port said, that by the law he has the right to put all shipwrecked mariners in jail, and to take all from them.

M. steamer Trent from leeward, we have received the intelligence, that a portion of the expedition which was formed for the invasion of the Island of Cuba, composed of about GUO adventurers, had succeeded in e fleeting a landing at a town about ten leagues east of Matanzas, which was however met and most signally defeated by Ihc loyalist troops. About four hundred of these men falling victims on the spot for their fool-hardiness ; whilst the remaining two hundred made a temporary escape to their vessels, but were subsequently captured by some of the Spanish cruizers. The aerounts respecting General Lopez, the leader, are conflicting, for whilst some statements mention his having been taken a prisoner, others say that he miraculously effected, with a few followers, his escape to a small island on the North Coast, w here he had been demanded by a Spanish commander; the Governor of the island refused however to deliver him up, preferring to await the arrival of an American man-of-war, whose Commander, it was thought, would order his delivery. þÿ St. Thomas Times.

Cuba axd her Destiny. þÿ Accounts recently received from Europe state that the Court of Madrid have given instructions to one of their agents Count Misarol, to make a thorough investigation into the island of Cuba, to ascertain the political sentiments of the inhabitants, and that if be found there was no probability of Spain being able to bold that island for any considerable time, he was authorised to enter into negotiation with the government at Washington for its transfer to the United States, for a reasonable price. The agent, it is said, has proceeded to Cuba, for the purpose of fulfilling his mission. About a year ago, perhaps longer, we impressed upon 1 i is Excellency M. Calderon de la llarea, the Spanish minister at Washington, the propriety of some such step as this, and requested him to communicate the same to his government. We were then, as we are now, perfectly satisfied, that the days þÿSpain s dominion over Cuba were numbered, and that sooner or later, in the natural course of things, that island would become part and parcel of the United States, by either annexation peaceably, or by negotiation, or by revolution, and annexation afterwards. We believe that his Excellency took the same view of the subject, for he could not but have known as well as we did, that such a result was inevitable, sooner or later, and as certain of being fulfilled as lhat the sun n\ ill rise to-morrow as usual in the East, and set again in the West. þÿ C.dderon de la llarea is a man of great

good sense and intellectual power ; he is a skilful diplomatist, and a person of accurate observation, lie is well acquainted with matters in the United States, and thoroughly conversant with the tone and course of public opinion here, especially on the subject of the island of Cuba. It' he has proposed, as we recommended, to the Court of Madrid, he has acted the part of a wise man, and the truth will be manifested before a very long time. It is therefore not unreasonable to expect that some proposition, emanating from the Spanish government, will ere long reach W ashington, in which the cession of the island of Cuba to the United States will be ordered for a fair consideration. Such a proposition ought to be favorably entertained by the government at Washington. The consideration or price is nothing in the scale, no matter how large might it be. The people of Cuba themselves would make it up, were it a hundred or a hundred and fifty millions of dollars. þÿ The advance in the value of property that would ensue would be sullicient to induce them to do so, apart from being released of the thirty millions of dollars per annum which the Spanish government extracts from them, without giving them any privilege in return. Cuba, once a State of this confederacy, would jump into a new existence. The people, being relieved of despotism, would , ut forth their energies, and in a short lime make it what nature designed it

3 T © 3C0 a £ AVI 3: should he þÿ one of the happiest, most i prosperous, and most wealthy countries in the world. Such a state of things as the cession of Cuba to this country is no doubt seriously entertained by the Spanish ministry. þÿ New York Herald.

New Mode of Crushing Sugar Cane. þÿ Yesterday morning a meeting took place at Baxter House, Old St. Paneras road, to witness an experiment, the result of Prince þÿAlbert o s ffer of a gold medal for the best improvement upon sugar-cane mills. The meeting consisted of a strong muster of planters from the West India colonies, several distinguished scientific men, and a special deputation from the Society of Arts. It appears that the most improved mode hitherto used for expressing the juice from the sugar canc is an arrangement of rollers worked by a steam-engine, through the former of which the sugar canes pass, and the juice is abstracted ; but from the porous nature of the cane fibre much of the juice is re-absorbed after the cane has passed through the rollers the practical result being that þÿ the most improved roller machines do not produce more than 5.3 per cent, of juice, whereas there is 90 per cent, in the cane. The first experiment made yesterday, resulted in abstracting the juice from 100 lb. of sugar-cane in OB seconds, only thrce-lourtbs of the actual power of the engine being exhibited. The second experiment was to test the amount of juice the engine was capable j of abstracting from a given weight of nine ; this was performed under disadvantageous circumstances, the cane having been cut upwards of four months since. 1\ ever' lieless, Go J lb. of juice was extracted from 100 lb. of cane, leaving little doubt but that under more favourable circumstances, the new engine

would realise 7.3 or 80 per cent, instead of the present average of .>.3 already mentioned þÿ an improvement of great magnitude and importance. Besides this, it was shown, that while the new mode of pressure completely abstracted the juice of the interior of the cane, its knot s and rind were left completely untouched þÿ a most important advantage, as it is there that the green wax and other objectionable matters are contained. The engine throughout was completely under control, and worked well ; and the greatest interest and excitement were evinced in the result of the experiment þÿ one certainly of great importance both to the West India interest and to the public at large. þÿ þÿBell s Messenger.

lO THE iVDITOR OF TIIE ST. CROIX AVIS. The Island of St. Croix. This beautiful and healthy place, so salubrious to the European, American, African and Native, is in þÿtruth þÿ the garden ot the AN est Indies. Its agreeable and wholesome climate invites manv to sojourn here, in order to recover lost health þÿ and its broad anil level roads so generally acknowledged to he superior to any others in the Westindia Islands, add considerably to the many comforts afforded to the stranger. And the small, but productive plantations, now happilycultivated by free labour, are thriving well, through the benign interposition ot the Almighty, and promise in time, by a continuation of His tender blessings and His heavenly protection, to reward the husbandman with a fair crop. These truths are very consoling, and inspire one with the desire of knowing something of the natives of this "sweet little spot J" What then is their character? Are they not injustice acknowledged to be an intellectual, well-disposed, moral people? Yes, I answer. But many of them, unfortunately, are left in the back þÿground arc looked they upon as undeserving, because fortune has frowned on them, and friends have either deserted them, or they never have found any þÿ they are forgotten as people holding dear and tender claims to the place of their birth, and are considered as having forfeited their birth-right. Why so? I ask. But it is better perhaps not to answer the question ; I must leave it to he answered by my fellownatives, who suffer as I do, and who do

not enjoy the privileges and advantages afforded to foreigners. Look around you in our public offices and institutions, and count the number of natives employed there! See if there are no more deserving of notice, and among the few, who have luckily attracted public attention, where do they stand? Have not the natives on many trying occasions evinced faithfully their zeal and loyalty towards (heir King and Country? Yes, I answer, and their praise-worthy acts must ever win for them the applause and approbation of every honest man. These relied ions are worthy ofattention, and as we must look forward to a future period for a better state of things, so do 1 sincerely wish that the natives will not rease to strive, as they hitherto have done, under the influence of existing salutary laws, by industry and perseverance, to prove themselves useful and worthy members of the eommunitv. S. Christiansted, Rd July 1850

NEW YORK. To the Editor of the Journal of Commerce. Grenvii.ee, S. C., May 1, 1850. Dear Sir: þÿ Although the winter lias been rather severe, and the spring remarkably cold anil wet, and protracted a month later than it was last year, yet T am happy to say the Tea Plant maintains its original physiology. The same laws which govern the plant in China, Java, and India, govern it here. Not a single deficiency in my small garden. þÿ livery plant has taken effective root, and early in April the leaf-buds came out in great profusion, all starting from the foot of the old leaf stalk. About the 20th April, the buds, influenced by increased temperature, followed their Chinese paternity, and began to develope an abundance of the most delicate leaves in regular season for the first gathering for the manufacture of the choicest quality of tea. Were it prudent to relax in the slightest degree the reciprocal action of root and branch, and thus delay the vigor, growth, blossom and fruiting of the natural plant, T could now gather a sufficient quantity of leaves to make a small supply of firstrate tea. But 1 compel myself to forbear the indulgence of a curiosity dear to my heart. The fact that the foliage puts out at the same time that it does in ( hina, affords another practical evidence of the adaptation of the American and the growth of the plant, climate to demonstrates the physiological fitness of a plant indigenous to China, to the culture of our own country. The final result depends upon our own industry, and we have not more ground for fear or appre-

hension of failure, than we have in transplanting a peach tree from France to America. The leaf is now of a light pea green color, and nothing can be imagined more tender and delicate. I can now understand why it is that we cannot obtain the first quality of tea from China. The first growth of the leaf is so delicate that it is quite impossible to divest it of humidity by firing or roasting to sustain so long a voyage, besides the almost certainty of utterly destroying its rich and precious aroma. I can now understand why it is that a Chinese official of wealth and dignity will pay a hundred dollars a pound for tea grown in his own country. The quantity of buds and early leaves, compared with a general gathering of leaves t'ullv grown, must be small indeed, and the value enhanced in proportion to the scarcity. We h ave to learn the effects of different soils, climate and locality, in the various tea growing districts of our own connfrv, both upon the growth of the plant and the quality of the tea. We have no reason to suppose that these effects will lie less diversified here than they are China ; but gathering instruction from the tea cultivators in China, Java, and India, 1 think we have no occasion to cultivate poor soil in a tropical climate, or one bordering upon it,

3 T $ 0 il £ ATH3, and thus produce an inferior quality of tea. We certainly ought to produce the best, and one of the inferior quality grown in China. In many respects we possess natural and peculiar advantages, which neither China nor Java nor India do or can possess. Our market, whether European or American, lies at outdoor. We are spared the expensive and injurious process of firing or roasting the tea leaf to prepare it for foreign markets. We have abundance of fine cheap lands, with all the diversity of soil, climate and aspect, that the plant can require. Our transportation, facilitated by rivers, canals and railroads, is so short to shipping ports, that the actual cost will not be one quarter so much as it is from the tea plantations of China to Canton, the port of shipment. More than all, every farmer, certainly in t lie Middle and Southern States, may grow his own tea in his own garden, without the slightest interference with his ordinary agricultural pursuits. With these exclusive privileges in our hands, if we do not cultivate our own tea, then I think we ought to be tributary to those who call us barbarians. Yours truly, JUNIUS SMITH.

The Standard of yesterday contains i the following account of the capture of the Brazilian brig, "Clementina," with Africans, by her Majesty's Schooner Bermuda, Lieut. Jolly. "The Bermuda, it seems, was at anchor in the Bight of Pines, oil' the Isle of Pines, on the Southside of Cuba, on the 20th ult., when a low suspicions looking brig was discovered outside steering for the land, but without shewing any colours. Suspecting the vessel to be a slaver, Lieut. Jolly, iinmediately got his little vessel underway, and stood out for the purpose of over-hauling and examining her. The brig, however, on discovering the Bermuda, at once altered her course, and made all sail off the land, the Bermuda in chase, and it was not until after a run of 40 hours, when the chase had made a considerable way into the Gulf of Mexico, that the Bermuda succeeded in disabling her, and making her a prize. In the course of the chase, eighty shots were fired from the Bermuda, many of which told on the rigging, which was eventually so disabled as to make her an easy prize. þÿ .She proved to be the Clementina, of Itio Janeiro, 170 tons, Brazilian measurement, commanded by Jose Gonzales Bandeira. She had on board when taken 280 slaves, of whom however several have died since their capture, from the state of debility in w hich they were in consequence of the want of food which was entirely out when she was captured. The vessel had Brazilian papers, dated in November, 1840, and prior to her surrender she hoisted
Brazilian colours. She had taken a Cuban pilot on board, and was about to land her cargo on the Isles of

Pines when discovered by her Majesty's Schooner. It is also stated that during the chase both vessels must have run upwards of three hundred miles, and that out of sixty rounds of shot fired from the Bf.r muda, not less than thirty-five took effect in the slaver's rigging, spars, and sails, such w as the precision of her gunnery ; motives of humanity caused the hull to be spared, as it was considered certain that a large number of Africans were confined below, among whom dreadful havoc must have been made had the Bermuda's shot been directed at the hull, besides running the risk oi sinking the brig. Such was the determination of the captain of the slaver, that he would not surrender until hi ; masts and rigging were cut to pieces by the Bermuda's fire ; and it was only when the helmsman's hat had been shot through and he quitted the wheel, followed by a volley of musketry from the Bermuda, that the captain would at last give in.

A question to Clergymen, Theologians, or to all others that can answer the same. It is eertainlv assumed to be settled 4 hat in the world, the natural as well as the spiritual, there is nothing that can be said to be unreasonable, i: e: which has not its use, its design, þÿ that every object, every idea in the natural and spiritual world consequently is useful and consistent. I enquire ot the consistency of the doctrine, embraced and authorized by the church, relative to the wise our Father and the Father Trinity. That God, our Creator, is ot like- all living þÿ the consistency oi this doctrine lean readily understand ; likewise that this Father of all would deliver his children from the dominion of Sin, and for that purpose has permitted a Person þÿ be lie His Son, a Prophet, or a moralreiigious Genius þÿ to appear among men to teach them their right relation to God, and thereby show them the way to salvation, and lastly 1 do likewise understand the consistency of a power or strength from the most High imparted to that mau who is fettered by sin, and thereby rendered weak, and who, instructed by the teachings of Christ, in repentance would desist from sin and turn himself to his God. He the doctrine of the Trinity explained in accordance herewith, then would I be able to perceive the consistency of such a Dogma ; but the doctrine of the Church on this subject, which arose in the third or fourth century and which was embraced by IiUther as an Article of belief, would

to the contrary be explained to teach that Jesus Christ is God, and the Iloly Ghost is God, both in conjunction w ith God the Father, and that these three Gods arc united in One and the same divine Essence þÿ an explanation, the consistency of which I can in no w ise comprehend, but to the contrary, I find it in the greatest measure inconsistent and pernicious, as it partly, to no purpose, gives us something to trouble our beads, and to wrangle about þÿ partly is " a rock of ofi'ence" to many both within and without Christendom. As this explanation has been prescribed for over 1500 years, we should believe that it was immoveable and the teachings on this subject consistent and useful, but as I and hundred thousands along with myself cannot perceive this, therefore, do I wish that the above-mentioned Gentlemen would for the good if the community, answer the proposed question, and so much more do I desire this, being myself a teacher of Religion; and I certainly cannot lake delight in

3 I. CS6I2 A 7 1 S> teaching children any thing, which according to my opinion, contradicts itselt bj its own inconsistency. In case the question should not be answered satisfactorily so that wc can clearly perceive the advantage of the Article of belief in question in the ac- þÿ ceptation of the Church þÿ so may we then commend the claim ot another question founded on this : Ought not the religious teaching in Schools, at least for children untill 12 þÿ 13 years ot age be given in its most simple style without being burthened with incomprehensible Dogmas, and a book ot tuition in this spirit occupy the place of that excessively dogmatical one ot Halle which apparently arose in a period, when it was feared that the Lutheran Dogmas would have been supplanted ? R. J. M.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, Having perused an article in your last paper signed S." 1 take the liberty, " with your permission to offer a few remarks thereon. The writer observes that " As we must look forward to a future period for a better state of things, so do 1 sincerely wish, that the natives will not cease to strive, as they hitherto have done, under the influence of existing salutary laws, by industry and perseverance, to prove themselves useful and worthy members of the community." We are all well aware, that the dissemination of learning, whether by proper schools or by the diffusion of accurate scientific knowledge by means of books, is one of the most powerful means of educating the people. þÿ Mow the native of this Island lias no such means in his power of becoming educated, even in a narrow sense of the term ; he has to contend against innumerable disadvantages, n ' should he feel the necessity " of knowing something more than the plainest rudiments of knowledge. He has to procure books suited to bis capacity and which could be of use to him without an instructor. Hut even should he procure these, then comes the tormenting conclusion, þÿ Of w hat use will it be for me to educate myself? What will be the reward for my toils ? None whatever. He can never hope for advancement. þÿ He can never aspire to anything great. Hut why ? Just because he was born in that very place, distinction in which lie aspires to, and because lie has never breathed the atmosphere of Europe,

which alone, apparently in the opinion of many, confers wisdom on, and fits for all situations, that happy being who has been fortunate enough to have been born there. 1 observed that the native lias to contend against disadvantages in procuring books suited to bis capacity and w hich could be of use to him without an instructor. This no one will deny. Where in this whole Island can any one purchase such a book? Where, in tact, can he procure any book at all? No where. Again, are there schools here

where lie could receive a liberal education? No. That the necessity even of such a school appears to have been denied, and that a more useful one was never "aimed at" will appear from what was observed by some one not long since, that when the established school here "Can send out children well grounded in acquirements generally taught in schools, viz : Religion, History and Geography, Arithmetic, Writing, Danish and English Reading and Orthography &.c. I relieve it accomplishes a ee which was aimed at as a Hcrgher school and we must rest satisfied therewith." Now observe, þÿ we must rest satisfied when the school sends out children well grounded in these things (which, en p ass ant, I have never yet had the pleasure of seeing,) and by so doing, it accomplishes all which was aimed at as a Hurgher school (a school for natives evidently, otherwise I am ignorant of the meaning.) It is evident from this that a landmark lias been set for the education of the native þÿ "thus far sbalt thou come and no further" is the language of this extract. Here is the sum-total of the education for the native. No more can he hope to receive, unless fortune favour his parents and he can be sent to breathe a little of that all-important European atmostphere ; never mind if as much care as he received here should be there bestowed on him, or if he should return as wise as he left,, there is now a little chance for him þÿ be may succeed \ i.ittle now, but far be the thought from him of aspiring to

anything as great as the foreigner. In conclusion, I would advise the natives, since, as it is said, the means of establishing a proper school :s not at command, to establish Libraries where the publications of such men as Messrs. Chambers «V Charles Knight may be kept for their use, and which could be procured by a trilling effort and for a small sum. Sl'ero meliora.

To the Editor of tiie St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, Your last number contains an article on the doctrine of the Trinity as held by the Christian Church, and makes the unfounded assertion that the present doctrine of the Church arose in the third or fourth century. If the communication should, as w as intended, aw aken doubts in any mind, perhaps the publication of the following Extract from þÿ þÿMoehler s Symbolism, þÿ may tend to allay those doubts and be interesting to some of your readers. The Oed Paths. þÿ þÿSwedenborg total s ignorance of ecclesiastical and dogmatic history, and bis presumption, in despite of this ignorance, to allege their testimony in support of his opinion, are particularly afflicting. lie ventures on the assertion, that from the time of the Apostles, down to this Council of Nice, his notion of the Trinity, was the prevailing belief of the Church, till of a sudden in this Council the true belief was lost! ! It is remarkable, withal, that elsewhere he includes

among the heretics of the first ages the Sabellians ; although it is precisely among these that lie might have found the most accurate resemblance to his own errors. In truth, had he known, that in the second and third centuries, the very few persons, who professed principles similar to his own, were menaced with exclusion from ecclesiastical communion, if they refused to renounce their opinions, utterly repugnant as they were to the universal doctrine of the Church : þÿ had lie been aware, that Praxeas was forced to exhibit a document, w herein lie revoked his error ; that Beryllus, at the Synod of Bostra, was prevailed upon by the Arabian bishops, as well as by Origen, w hom they had summoned to their aid, to take the same step ; and, that Sabellius excited such great agitation in the Egyptian Church, and became the object of such general abhorrence ; how could lie have had the hardihood to put forth the assertion, that þÿdow to n the Council of Nice, his opinion was the faith of the Church! If, in modern days, many since the time of Souveriin have asserted, that the ante- Niccnc period was addicted to the Ariau heresy ; a superficial study of authorities, at least, might have led to such a result ; but þÿSwedenborg s assertion, presupposes the utter absence of all historical inquiry. Yet a book, in which such gross and palpable errors are found, lie dares to extol as a work of such Divine contents, that on its completion, the Apostles entered upon a mission through the whole spiritual world; that

on its publication, the very salvation of futurity depends ; and that with it commences the new eternal Church þÿ! þÿ Of what is called Scriptural proof, Swedenborg has not the slightest notion. It is a mere accident, if in support ol any one, even ot his truest propositions, lie assigns satisfactory excgetical grounds. 11c usually heaps passages upon passages, without much troubling himself about usage of speech, the context, parallel passages, or in general, the strict application of hermeneutic rules, although with these, he was not unacquainted. It is so in the matter under discussion. Let any one only read the passages he cites from Isaiah, Jeremiah, Osce, and the Psalms, in order to prove, that it was not the Son begotten of the Father from all eternity, hut he, whom lie calls Jehovah, that became Man and Redeemer ; and, such a one must he convinced, that w ith a like course of reasoning, any conceivable fancy of the brain, might be supported by þÿScripture. From the St Thomas Times, June 26, 1850. The Bermuda Gazette, of the? I8th instant, furnishes us with the following important article relating to Cuba. From the N. V. Courier and Enquirer June 5. litj Magnetic Telegraph. Washington, Jrine 4. The Union states, that it understands despatches have been received by the government from our Consul at Havana, stating that he had demanded the 105 persons taken by a Spanish ship-of-war on tiie Island of Cantroy. Cantroy is a neutral territory, and ihe men taken there had not been engaged in open hostilities, and were actually considering the propriety of abandoning the enterprise and returning to the United States. The Governor has made no reply to our Consul, who had transmitted despatches to Washington, stating the facts, and calling for additional power to second his demand. Despatches were yesterday sent to such portions of our squadron, as could be immediately collected at Havana, to assist in pressing the demand. Should the Spanish Government refuse, the Consul is instructed to inform our Government, and, meantime, our vessels of war are to obstruct communication of all vessels with the port. It is reported, two vessels with reinforcements for General I.opez, which were commissioned to land at different points of the Island, are still at sea þÿ their fate and destination unknown. It is said that in the event of these vessels being captured by the Spanish, our own squadron, is instructed to demand them of the Spanish commander, and if not given up, to seize them by force.

New York Herat. n. Oisr Jamaica Correspondence. Jamaica, May 12, 1850. Gen. Paez Coming to New York. We have lately received news here from Ycnezucla, communicating the pleasing intelligence that General Jose Antonio Paez, the distinguished citizen of Venezuela, is to be sent on board of the Venezuclian schooner Intrepid, from Cumana, to New York, on the 15th May inst. In all probability, you will see in your city in the latter part of this May, or the beginning of June next, this venerable patriot, the companion in arms of Gen. Bolivar. As General Paez has a historic name, and has done so much in favor of the cause of independence and of civil liberty in this part of the world, I have no doubt he will be welcomed, and properly received and appreciated in the United States, that home of the free and asylum of the oppressed.

CUBA. Our columns supply the most ample and satisfactory intelligence with respect to the failure of the invasion of Cuba. þÿ The accounts are derived from three sources þÿ the invaders themselves, from the Spanish authorities, and from disinterested persons. They all agree with each other, and establish, beyond the conjecture of a doubt, the total failure of the expedition. Thus this absurd and silly attempt to stimulate an insurrection, where the people have shown that it was not desired, has proved a serious sacrilice to life, that must always be referred to as extremely criminal on the part ol those who have been engaged in favoring it. The lesson is a humiliating one ; but it is also one that may be profitable to our countrymen. It is possible that an expedition may be started for another point. A letter writer of the cabinet at Washington, has announced that the government is informed that two vessels are fitting out for Hayti one at Boston, the other þÿ here þÿ to assist Fussy the First, against the Dominicans. The boot is probably, on the other leg, in spite of the golden boots of the emperor. The expedition

is to assist the Dominicans, who are at the mercy of the black autocrat. This may turn out very differently from the Cuban affair, because we have no treaty with Hayti þÿ no understanding þÿ have been subjected to insults, and no foreign power can interfere in the matter. þÿ Should the ambitious idlers of the population of the two cities determine to make the attempt, we see no reason to believe that they will not change the complexion of the government. The plan has been long talked of, and we know not what may be the result. þÿ Cuba may remain as it is: but Hayti seems destined to undergo a change. þÿ lb.
