To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, 1 perused, in your last paper, a communication inserted for the purpose of allaying any doubts that may have arisen in any mind on the doctrine of the Trinity, which doubts, it was feared, might have arisen from the question to Theologians &c. inserted in your paper of the 8ih. From the manner in which this communication commences, I of course expected that the writer, feeling for the state of miml ol this Clergyman, intended to explain the doctrine of the Trinity anti to show what that Clergyman desires to perceive ; viz; þÿ the consistency and reasonableness of the docþÿtrine. Such a course of procedure ought naturally to have been adopted by 11 The old paths but what has lie done to remove the doubts of this Clergyman and þÿ to allay those of your readers?" Why he has attacked a body of Christians, who hail nothing at all to do with the matter, except in so far that they, to my knowledge, ate the only class of Christians who can clear up those doubts and show the consistency and reasonableness of this doctrine, in order to disperse these doubts your correspondent has published a quotation from the work of a Roman Catholic Professor of Theology against Swedenborg and his doctrines, io which work the writer has taken the doctrines of his Church as a standard of truth by which to judge of the truth of the doctrines of Protestants and others, and who unblushingly declares that þÿ The authority of the Church (of Rome) is the medium of all, which in the

Christian religion resteth on authority, and is so far an authority as the Church is an authority authority, that is to say, the Christian reli- gion itself ; so that Christ himself is only in Leaving this introductory piece of the þÿ . old paths" we will at once proceed to examine the misrepresentations of Doctor Moehler ; merely requesting the reader to take notice that although Swedenborg has written some thirty large octavo volumes on theological subjects, Dr. Moehler confesses that he had only read one solitary work of that author which is now published in a single octavo volume. Dr. Moehler begins by charging Swedenborg with total ignorance of ecclesiastical and dogmatic history. Now that a man of such learning and deep research as Swedenborg was, should not have been acquainted with history, is a charge that every unprejudiced man must doubt. No one who has ever read the Eulogium to his memory that was pronounced in the great hall of the House of Nobles, in the name of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Stockholm, by M Sandel, can fail to perceive that this charge must be unfounded. Dr. Moehler soys that þÿ Swedenborg ventures on the assertion, that from the time of the Apostles, down to the Council of Nice, his notion of the Trinity, was the prevailing belief of the Church, Till of a sudden, in this Council the true belief was lost ! þÿI Swedenborg does declare that þÿ A Trinity of persons was unknown in the Apostolic Church." Now if the Apostles taught such
a doctrine, they would evidently have made mention of it in their Epistles ; but this we assert that a Trinity of Persons, can no where be discovered in them, but to the

contrary we find that although the Apostles were commanded to þÿ Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the namp of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy þÿSpirit þÿ yet they, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, baptized in the name of Jesus only. This is something more than presumptive evidence, that they considered the entire Divinity to be lodged in his person, for when he directed them to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, they immediately went and baptized in his name only ; never dreaming that they were called upon to make any 9uch distinction into persons, as was afterwards invented, but simply to direct their thoughts, their hearts, and their worship, to the single person of Jesus alone. Should þÿ the old paths" think that the writings of the Apostles or any other part of the word of God teach the doctrine of three persons in the Trinity, tie will be conferring a favour on me by bringing such passages to view. That Swedenborg is not alone in asserting that at the Council of Nice the doctrine of a Trinity of Persons was broached will appear from the following quotation from the work of Wm. B. Hayden in reply to Dr. Fond, Professor in the Theological Seminary at Bangor, Maine, who raised this very objection. þÿ There are two doctrines of the Trinity: the one that the three Essentials of the Godhead reside in one Person ; which is the doctrine of Swedenborg; and, as we claim, of the Scriptures, and may be called the

Trinity in Unity. The other that three distinct Persons enter into the Godhead, which is the doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church distinguished as the Tri-personal þÿ Trinity, and may be called the Unity in Trinity. Now when Dr. Pond asserts that the doctrine of the Trinity is taught in the Bible, we of course agree with him. When ho says it is easy to prove its existence before the Nicene Council, we agree w ith him. But when he goes on to assert, what is not found in Scripture, that those three are distinct persons, and not os we believe, three names applied to the same person, then we part company with him and deny it. If he means that this Tri-personal Trinity is the one which was taught before the Nicene Council, we are at direct issue with him on the question of fact. It is rather strange too that he should state positively that it is as easy to prove the Tri-personal Trinity before the Nicene Council as after it; when it is well known that it cannot be done. þÿ Among the many authorities which might be cited on this subject, a single one of high standing will be sufficient. We extract from Mr. John Henry þÿNewman Essay s on »he Development of Christian Doctrine þÿ Speaking of the doctrine of the Trinity, before the Nicene Council, he say's Now let þÿ us look at the leading facts of the case; first, the creeds of that early day make no mention of the Catholic doctrine at all. They make mention indeed of a Three ; but that there is any mystery in the doctrine, that

the three are one, that they are co-equal, coeternal, all uncreate, all omnipotent, all incomprehensible. is r.ot stated, and never could be gathered from them!' We could give lengthy quotations to the same effect, more fully discussing the point and adducing the authorities. Those who wish to pursue rt further, will find the subject ably drawn

35. C 3$ A3U. out in Mr. þÿNewman s introduction. We have referred to him, because whatever we may think of the theology of the Oxford school, they possess the very highest authority in matters of ecclesiastical history, and moreover cannot be suspected of any ISwedenborgian bias. What Mr. Newman says of the creeds, applies equally to the writings of the early fathers, and all other ante- Nicene documents; and his assertion is that the Catholic doctrine of the Tri-personal Trinity 11 cannot be made out from any of them in the prayer of St. Chrysostom as

of the Church of England, not the slightest intimation of a Tri-personal doctrine is in the remotest degree alluded to ; and this is beyond all doubt to be attributed to tire fact that Chrysostom wrote anterior to the Nicene Council, when no such doctrine as modern Tripersonalism was entertained in the true Church of Christ. We say modern Tripersonaiism, because the doctrine of three persons is a perversion of the original Nicene Creed ns written in tire Gieek Language ; which, was only introduced when said Creed was translated into the modern Languages of Europe. Dr Moehler next charges Swedenborg with holding a doctrine similar by Sabelliunisnr. It is similar in the fact that it denies the tri -personality of the Godhead, but it is quite dilfercut in other respects Sabellius held that the terms Father, Son and Holy Ghost were merely the names of a three- fold manifestation of the one undistinguished es- j judgment of the candid render who has ever sence of the Deity. Swedenborg, on the other hand, maintains a fundamental distinction of the principles of Love, Wisdom and Operation, in the very inmost of the Divine Being, and that the names Father, Son and Holy Ghost have relation respectively to these three principles, which however arc as far from constituting three distinct persons as Soul, Body and Operation, or Action in man are from constituting turn individually, thiee persons þÿ By þÿFather, says Mr. Noble, when mentioned in Scripture, is not meant a God distinct from Jesus Christ, but His

inmost principle of Divine life, answering (to compare things infinite with things finite) to the soul in man. By the Son is not meant a Divine Being separate from the Father, but the manifested Form of the Divine Essence answering to the body in man. And by tire Holy Spirit is not meant a Divine Person distinct from both, but the operating life or influence of the Divine Essence and the Di vine Form in union, answering to the operating faculty in man, or to the influence which he exercises upon persons and things within his sphere of action. Thus the whole Divine Trinity centres in the one undivided person of the Lord Jesus Christ ; and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit no more form three divine persons or Gods, than soul, body and operation, in each of us, form three | human persons in þÿman. For further information on this subject we refer tire reader to þÿNoble Appeal, s Appendix No. H. What hose calumny ! þÿ 1 can scarcely think it possible that Dr, Moehler was not aware, while writing ibis that he was uttering a falsehood þÿ 1 am so much more certain of this from the fact that in that very translation of this work, (viz , þÿ True Christian Religion") which he used, there is a note referring to this very same passage, to guard the reader from supposing that by the þÿ þÿwork of which Swedenborg speaks, he meant the work which he wrote, but that by the work here alluded to, we are to understand the work of Uedemption, and the formation of a introduced into the Book of common Pray er ' New Angelic Heaven in the spiritual world, as will be evident to any one who will refer to Nos. 4 108, lg3 and 784 of this work þÿ In order to prove more fully that by the wotk mentioned by Swedcnboig in this Memorandum rt 701, he does not mean the work which he wrote, ns Dr. Moehler would have us to believe, 1 will note this circumstance that in the 'cry first Chapter of this work n. 4 Swedenborg speaks of this Mission of the Apostles as having already token place not many months þÿago, consequently before he ever commenced writing this wotk which Dr Moehler says that he alludes to in this Memorandum. Dr. Moehler fuither remarks þÿ þÿ Of what is called Scriptural proof, Swedenborg lias not the slightest notion. It is a mete accident if in support of any one, even of his exegetical truest propositions, he þÿ grounds Ac assigns satisfactory How true this is, we will leave to the

read any of þÿSwedenborg w s orks, or any of the works published by those who believe in the truth of his writings. How true this statement is. can likewise fie seen fiom the fact that Swedenborg frequently declares that The doctrine of the Church ought to be drawn from the litem/ sense of Word, and to be confirmed there- the by;" which rule be strictly follows throughout all his works and is exceprionably singular in tbai respec\ Dr Moehler likewise observes : þÿ Let anv one only read the passages he cites from Isaiah, Jeremiah, (Lee. and the Psalms, in order to prove that it w as not the Son begotten of the Father from all eternity, but he, whom lie calls Jehovah, that her nine Man and Redeemer and such a one must be convinced. that with a like course of reasoning anv conceivable fancy of the brain, might be supported by þÿscripture.
